test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 22 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: Which statement about parallel connection of resistors is true?

options.text: Each resistor carries the same current regardless of its resistance.
The total current is the sum of the currents through individual resistors.
The total current is the same as current through any branch.
The total resistance increases when more resistors are added.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The total current is the sum of the currents through individual resistors**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In a **parallel connection**, all the resistors are connected between the same two common points or nodes. This ensures that the **potential difference (Voltage)** across each individual resistor remains the same.
 
• According to **Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL)**, the total current entering a junction must be equal to the sum of the currents leaving that junction. In a parallel circuit, the **total current (I)** provided by the source divides among the various branches.
 
• The mathematical expression for total current in a parallel circuit is **I = I1 + I2 + I3 + ... + In**. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• In a parallel circuit, the current through each resistor is determined by **Ohm's Law (I = V/R)**. Since the voltage (V) is constant, the current is inversely proportional to the **resistance (R)**. This means resistors with different values will carry different currents. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• The total current is the aggregate of all branch currents, meaning it cannot be the same as the current through a single branch unless there is only one resistor in the circuit. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• Adding more resistors in parallel provides additional paths for the electric current to flow. This reduces the overall opposition to the current, meaning the **equivalent resistance decreases** as more resistors are added. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Equivalent Resistance (Req):** The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances. The formula is **1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + ... + 1/Rn**.
 
• **Smallest Resistance Rule:** One of the unique features of parallel circuits is that the **total equivalent resistance** is always **smaller than the smallest individual resistance** present in the parallel network.
 
• **Domestic Wiring:** In most **households**, electrical appliances are connected in **parallel**. This ensures that every device receives the full supply voltage (usually **220V to 240V** depending on the **country**) and can be operated independently using its own switch.
 
• **Fault Tolerance:** Parallel circuits are highly reliable for complex systems. If one resistor or appliance in a parallel branch burns out or is disconnected, the **other branches remain unaffected** and continue to operate normally because their circuits are still complete.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Comparison with Series Circuits:** In a **series circuit**, the **current** remains the same through all components, while the **total voltage** is the sum of the individual voltage drops across the resistors. This is the exact opposite of a parallel circuit.
 
• **Power Dissipation:** The total **power (P)** consumed by a parallel circuit is the sum of the power dissipated by each individual resistor. Since **P = V² / R**, the resistor with the **lowest resistance** will dissipate the **highest power** in a parallel connection.
 
• **Current Division Rule:** For two resistors (**R1** and **R2**) in parallel, the current through **R1** is calculated as **I1 = I * (R2 / (R1 + R2))**, where **I** is the total current. This highlights how current distribution is dependent on the ratio of resistances.
